chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from a man, from Safwan, who said:

I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who left Baghdad intending to catch up with a man who was one mile ahead, and he kept following him until he reached al-Nahrawan, which is four farsakhs from Baghdad. Should he break his fast if he intends to return, and shorten his prayer? He said: 'He does not shorten [prayer] and he does not break his fast, because he left his home intending [only] to catch up with his companion on part of the road, and the journey extended him to the place he reached. And if he had left his home intending al-Nahrawan going and returning, it would have been upon him to intend travel and breaking his fast from the night. But if he set out in the morning and did not intend travel, and it became apparent to him after morning that he was traveling, he shortens [prayer] and does not break his fast on that day.'

key_terms.الرِّضَا عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: Al-Rida (peace be upon him), referring to Imam Ali al-Rida
key_terms.النَّهْرَوَانَ: Al-Nahrawan, a specific location near Baghdad
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: Farsakhs, a unit of distance measurement

ai.seo_question: Does a traveler need to intend to break their fast the night before if they start traveling from home in the morning?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that the ruling of *qasr* (shortening prayer) and *iftar* (breaking fast) depends on the initial intention (*niyyah*) at the time of departure rather than the final distance covered. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that a local traveler who exceeds the threshold of *safar* (eight parasangs) without prior intent remains a resident for fasting purposes, whereas one who intends the long journey from the outset is considered a traveler. This hadith is pivotal in understanding the flexibility of ritual obligations based on the traveler's state of mind and origin.
